title: Quantum mechanics II
summary: Stationary and time-dependent perturbation theory, the variational method, identical particles, atomic structure, scattering, and entanglement.
overview: Hydrogen is the last realistic system whose Schrödinger equation can be solved exactly. Everything else, from helium to a laser-driven atom to a neutron striking a nucleus, needs controlled approximations, and this course develops the standard ones: perturbation theory for small corrections to a solvable Hamiltonian, the variational method for ground states when no small parameter exists, and the Born and partial-wave approximations for scattering. Alongside them it develops two structural facts that no approximation may violate: identical particles are indistinguishable, so their states are symmetric or antisymmetric, and the state of a composite system need not be a product of states of its parts.

The first two chapters treat perturbations that are constant in time, giving energy shifts such as the fine structure of hydrogen and the Zeeman and Stark effects, and perturbations that change in time, giving Rabi oscillations, Fermi's golden rule and the rates of emission and absorption of light. The next two build atoms: exchange symmetry and the Pauli principle, the exchange energy that separates helium's singlet and triplet states, and then the central-field approximation, Hund's rules and the periodic table. The fifth chapter returns to the continuum with cross sections, Rutherford's formula and phase shifts. The last treats density matrices and entanglement, Bell's theorem and the CHSH inequality, and the no-cloning theorem and teleportation that underlie quantum information.

The mathematics is the linear algebra and angular momentum of Quantum Mechanics I, used hard. The main difficulty is bookkeeping: knowing which states are unperturbed and which are exact, which basis diagonalises a perturbation, which quantities are first order and which second. Every lesson checks its approximations against an exact result or an experiment (helium's ground-state energy, the lifetime of hydrogen's 2p state, the Rutherford cross section, the measured violation of Bell's inequality), and doing the same with your own calculations is the best way to learn the subject.
outcomes: Derive and apply the first- and second-order energy corrections of non-degenerate perturbation theory, and diagonalise a perturbation within a degenerate subspace.
Compute the fine structure of hydrogen and the Zeeman and Stark shifts of its levels, with numbers.
Use the variational principle to bound ground-state energies, including the screened-charge estimate for helium.
Solve the driven two-level system, derive Fermi's golden rule, and compute electric-dipole transition rates and lifetimes with the Einstein coefficients.
Construct symmetric and antisymmetric states of identical particles, apply the Pauli principle, and explain the exchange energy of helium's singlet and triplet states.
Explain the shell structure of atoms and the periodic table from the central-field approximation, and find ground-state term symbols with Hund's rules.
Compute differential cross sections in the Born approximation and with phase shifts, derive Rutherford's formula, and prove the optical theorem.
Describe entangled states with density matrices and the Schmidt decomposition, prove the CHSH inequality and Tsirelson's bound, and explain no-cloning and teleportation.

chapters.title: Stationary perturbation theory
chapters.summary: Non-degenerate and degenerate perturbation theory, the fine structure of hydrogen, the Zeeman and Stark effects, and the variational method.

chapters.title: Time-dependent perturbation theory
chapters.summary: Rabi oscillations, first-order transition amplitudes, Fermi's golden rule, and the absorption and emission of light.

chapters.title: Identical particles
chapters.summary: Exchange symmetry, the Pauli principle, the exchange force, and the singlet and triplet states of helium.

chapters.title: Atoms
chapters.summary: The central-field approximation, Hartree–Fock, the periodic table, term symbols and Hund's rules.

chapters.title: Scattering
chapters.summary: Cross sections, the Born approximation, Rutherford's formula, partial waves and the optical theorem.

chapters.title: Entanglement and measurement
chapters.summary: Density matrices, the EPR argument, Bell's theorem and the CHSH inequality, no-cloning and teleportation.

history.title: The exclusion principle
history.detail: Wolfgang Pauli proposed that no two electrons in an atom can have the same four quantum numbers, explaining the closing of atomic shells; the fourth quantum number was identified with spin later that year.

history.title: Rayleigh–Schrödinger perturbation theory
history.detail: In the third of his papers on quantisation as an eigenvalue problem, Erwin Schrödinger adapted Rayleigh's method for perturbed vibrations to wave mechanics, including degenerate levels, and applied it to the Stark effect of hydrogen.

history.title: Born's collision theory
history.detail: Max Born treated scattering in wave mechanics, obtaining the first-order Born approximation and, in the same work, interpreting the square of the wavefunction as a probability density.

history.title: Dirac's theory of radiation
history.detail: Paul Dirac quantised the electromagnetic field and derived the rates of emission and absorption, including spontaneous emission, using the time-dependent perturbation theory he had developed in 1926.

history.title: The Hartree–Fock method
history.detail: Douglas Hartree's self-consistent field of 1928 was made antisymmetric by Vladimir Fock and John Slater in 1930, giving the standard starting point for atomic and molecular structure calculations.

history.title: EPR and entanglement
history.detail: Einstein, Podolsky and Rosen argued that quantum mechanics is incomplete because it assigns no definite values to quantities that can be predicted with certainty at a distance; Schrödinger named the phenomenon entanglement the same year.

history.title: The golden rule named
history.detail: Enrico Fermi's Chicago lecture notes on nuclear physics called the transition-rate formula derived by Dirac "Golden Rule No. 2", and the name stuck.

history.title: Bell's theorem
history.detail: John Bell proved that no local hidden-variable theory can reproduce the quantum correlations of the spin singlet. Clauser, Horne, Shimony and Holt gave the experimentally practical CHSH form in 1969.

history.title: Aspect's experiments
history.detail: Alain Aspect and colleagues measured violations of Bell's inequality with entangled photons, in one experiment switching the analyser settings while the photons were in flight.

history.title: Loophole-free Bell tests
history.detail: Groups at Delft, Vienna and NIST closed the detection and locality loopholes simultaneously. In 2022 Aspect, Clauser and Zeilinger received the Nobel Prize in Physics for experiments with entangled photons.

references.title: Introduction to Quantum Mechanics
references.authors: David J. Griffiths and Darrell F. Schroeter
references.note: Third edition. The clearest undergraduate account of perturbation theory, the variational principle, identical particles, quantum dynamics and scattering, with many worked problems.

references.title: Modern Quantum Mechanics
references.authors: J. J. Sakurai and Jim Napolitano
references.note: Third edition. The graduate-level step up: the projection and Wigner–Eckart theorems, the interaction picture, Lippmann–Schwinger scattering theory and density operators.

references.title: Principles of Quantum Mechanics
references.note: Second edition. Careful on the mathematical formalism, with good chapters on perturbation theory, identical particles and scattering.

references.title: Physics of Atoms and Molecules
references.authors: B. H. Bransden and C. J. Joachain
references.note: Second edition. The standard reference for atomic structure: fine structure, radiative transitions, two-electron atoms, the central field, Hartree–Fock and term symbols.

references.title: Quantum Computation and Quantum Information
references.authors: Michael A. Nielsen and Isaac L. Chuang
references.note: Tenth-anniversary edition. Density operators, the Schmidt decomposition, Bell inequalities, no-cloning and teleportation in the language of quantum information.

references.title: Quantum Mechanics, Volume 2
references.authors: Claude Cohen-Tannoudji, Bernard Diu and Franck Laloë
references.note: Second edition. Exhaustive and careful; the complements on fine structure, the Zeeman effect and atom–light interaction are worth looking up when a shorter argument feels too quick.

references.title: Speakable and Unspeakable in Quantum Mechanics
references.note: Second edition. Bell's papers on the foundations of quantum mechanics, including the 1964 theorem, collected and written with unusual clarity.
